name: Eastern Nepal
tagline: Tea hills, Kirat villages, Kanchenjunga's quiet side
meta_description: Eastern Nepal travel guide: Ilam tea country, Kanchenjunga and Makalu treks, Pathibhara, Dhankuta and Hile, Kirat culture. When to go, how to reach, permits.
summary: Eastern Nepal is the Koshi hills: Ilam's tea gardens, the Kanchenjunga and Makalu base camp treks, the pilgrim summit of Pathibhara and the ridge towns of Dhankuta and Hile. It is the homeland of the Kirat Rai and Limbu, far quieter than Everest or Annapurna, and best from October to May.
intro: Most visitors to Nepal go west from Kathmandu, toward Pokhara and the Annapurnas, or north-east to Everest. Eastern Nepal gets a small share of them, which is part of its appeal. Between the Arun river and the Indian border lie green hills of tea and cardamom, ridge-top bazaars, deep river valleys and, to the north, Kanchenjunga and Makalu, the third and fifth highest mountains on earth.

This is Kirat country. The Rai and the Limbu (Yakthung) are among Nepal's oldest peoples, with their own languages, the Limbu script, and the Mundhum, an oral scripture recited by their priests. Their festivals, Sakela and Chasok Tangnam, follow the farming year, and their food, from kinema to tongba, is found nowhere else in Nepal in the same way.

Travel here comes in two kinds. In the hills, short and gentle trips: Ilam and Kanyam for tea, Sandakpur for the view of four of the five highest peaks, Dhankuta and Hile for ridge-town life. In the high north, long and serious treks: Kanchenjunga's north base camp at Pang Pema, and Makalu Base Camp through the forests of the Barun.

Distances are long and roads are slow, so plan for fewer places and more days. A week covers Ilam's tea country and Sandakpur. Ten days lets you add Dhankuta, Hile and Chainpur. The big treks need two to three weeks each. Flights to Bhadrapur, Biratnagar and Tumlingtar save days of driving.

story.title: The Kirat hills between the Arun and the Mechi
paras: Long before the kingdom of Nepal existed, these hills were Kirat land. Rai communities lived mainly in the middle hills, the region often called Khambuwan or Majh Kirat, and the Limbu in the far east, Limbuwan or Pallo Kirat, east of the Arun. Limbuwan was traditionally divided among ten chiefdoms. Each people kept its own languages, clans, priests and oral traditions, gathered in the Mundhum.

In the late 18th century the Gorkhali state of Prithvi Narayan Shah expanded east and brought the Kirat hills into the new kingdom. Limbu chiefs kept a degree of local authority for many decades under the kipat system of communal land, though later reforms eroded it. In the 18th century the Limbu scholar Te-ongsi Sirijunga revived and taught the Limbu script, which is still named after him.

The modern east grew with tea, roads and soldiers. Tea was planted in Ilam in the 1860s. Men from these hills joined the Gurkha regiments of the British and Indian armies, and their pensions built houses across Dhankuta and Dharan. Roads arrived late: the Dharan–Dhankuta highway was completed in 1982, and many valleys toward Kanchenjunga and Makalu have been reached by jeep only in the last two decades.

Conservation came too. Makalu Barun National Park was created in 1992, and the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area in 1997. In 2006 the management of Kanchenjunga was handed to a council of local people, one of the first such handovers in Nepal. Since 2015 the region has formed part of Koshi Province, with its capital at Biratnagar.

legend: The Limbu Mundhum tells how Tagera Ningwaphumang, the supreme creator, made the world, and how Yuma Sammang, the ancestral grandmother goddess, became the guardian of the Limbu home and its people. She is honoured at every Chasok Tangnam with the first grain of the harvest. Rai traditions in the Mundhum tell their own creation stories and of ancestors who moved up and down the hills with the seasons, a journey remembered in the Sakela dance.
people: Eastern Nepal is home to Rai and Limbu (Yakthung) communities, with Brahmin, Chhetri, Newar, Tamang, Magar, Gurung, Sherpa, Sunuwar, Yakkha and Lepcha families among many others, and Buddhists of Tibetan descent in high villages such as Ghunsa. Rai alone speak many languages, including Bantawa, Kulung and Athpare. People farm rice, millet, maize, cardamom, tea and oranges, and many families depend on work abroad.

untold.fact: Mundhum, the oral scripture of the Limbu, is said to mean the power of great strength in the Limbu language, and is organised into two parts, Thungsap and Peysap.
Kinema, a fermented soybean food also called hongema or hokima, is a traditional food of the Limbu people and is now also made by other Kirat communities of eastern Nepal, Sikkim and Darjeeling.
Te-ongsi Sirijunga, an 18th-century Limbu scholar of Limbuwan and Sikkim, revived and taught the Limbu script, which is widely known as the Sirijanga script after him.
Kanchenjunga's name was explained in the 19th century by the Schlagintweit brothers as meaning the five treasures of the high snow, from Tibetan words.
Bhadrapur's airport in Jhapa, the main air gateway to Ilam's tea country, has served as an airfield since November 1963.

taste.name: Kinema
taste.text: Soybeans boiled, wrapped in leaves and left to ferment for a few days, then cooked as a curry or pickle with tomato and chilli. Strong-smelling, savoury and very Limbu. Ask for it in local kitchens in Taplejung, Ilam, Dhankuta and Dharan, and at village homestays.

highlights.title: Ilam and Kanyam tea country
highlights.text: Walk the rows of Nepal's oldest tea gardens at dawn, taste first and autumn flush in Ilam bazaar, and see Kanyam's open slopes before the weekend crowds. Two or three gentle days at 1,300–1,600 m.

highlights.title: Sandakpur's four-peak sunrise
highlights.text: From 3,636 m on the Nepal–India border, see Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga in one sunrise. From the Ilam side it is a long jeep day or a 3–5 day walk through rhododendron forest.

highlights.title: Pang Pema, Kanchenjunga north
highlights.text: One of Nepal's great remote treks, through Limbu villages and the Tibetan Buddhist village of Ghunsa to Pang Pema at about 5,143 m, under the north face of the world's third highest mountain.

highlights.title: Makalu Base Camp and the Barun
highlights.text: From the warm Arun valley near Tumlingtar over the Shipton La to the Barun valley and Makalu's south face at about 4,870 m, through some of the richest forests in the Himalaya.

highlights.title: Pathibhara Devi pilgrimage
highlights.text: Climb with pilgrims before dawn to the goddess shrine at 3,794 m above Taplejung, known to the Limbu as Mukkumlung, with views to Kanchenjunga on clear mornings.

highlights.title: Ridge towns of the Koshi hills
highlights.text: Dhankuta's calm bazaar and winter oranges, Hile's tongba kitchens and misty ridge, Bhedetar's view over the plains and Chainpur's brass workshops: slow travel on the road north from Dharan.

getting_there: Eastern Nepal has three useful airports. Bhadrapur in Jhapa, about 45–50 minutes by air from Kathmandu, is the gateway to Ilam, Kanyam, Sandakpur and, by a long drive north, Taplejung and Pathibhara. Biratnagar, about 40 minutes from Kathmandu with frequent flights, serves Dharan, Bhedetar, Dhankuta and Hile. Tumlingtar, about 45 minutes from Kathmandu, is the gateway to Chainpur and the Makalu trek, though its flights are more often hit by weather. By road, the East–West Highway runs along the Terai, with the Mechi Highway climbing north to Ilam and Taplejung and the Koshi Highway climbing from Dharan to Dhankuta, Hile and Khandbari. Overnight buses from Kathmandu take 10–16 hours to the eastern towns. Hill roads are slow and can be blocked by monsoon landslides. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Most of eastern Nepal needs no trekking permit: Ilam, Kanyam, Sandakpur's Nepal side, Pathibhara, Dhankuta, Hile, Bhedetar, Tumlingtar and Chainpur are open. The Kanchenjunga region requires a Kanchenjunga Conservation Area permit and a restricted area permit, issued through a registered agency, normally for at least two trekkers with a licensed guide. The Makalu trek requires a Makalu Barun National Park permit. Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas to trek with a licensed guide. Fees and rules change; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Ilam about 3–16 °C, dry, clear, frosty mornings
months.summary: Cold, dry and clear in the hills, with some of the sharpest mountain views of the year from Antu Danda and the ridges above Ilam and Hile. Tea bushes rest, so the gardens are quiet. Oranges are still on sale in Dhankuta. Sandakpur is very cold with possible snow, and the high Kanchenjunga and Makalu treks are effectively closed. A good month for warm, sunny days in Tumlingtar and the Arun valley.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for evenings in Ilam and Hile even if days feel mild.

months.summary: Still cool and dry, with lengthening days. Hill towns are quiet and views remain good in the mornings, though haze starts to build late in the month. Tea gardens are pruned and green leaf is weeks away. The high passes such as the Shipton La are usually snowbound. Lhosar, the Tibetan New Year, may fall this month in Buddhist villages, depending on the lunar calendar.
months.tip: Combine Ilam and Kanyam with a sunrise at Antu Danda while the air is still clear.

months.summary: Spring arrives. Rhododendrons start to flower on the lower ridges, and the first flush of tea begins in the last week of the month. Pilgrims gather at Pathibhara for Chaite Dashain when it falls in March. Mountain views are hazier than in autumn but still good in the early morning. High treks open later in the month as snow clears from the lower passes.
months.tip: Book Pathibhara lodges early if your dates overlap Chaite Dashain.

months.weather: Ilam about 13–24 °C, warm days, afternoon showers
months.summary: Rhododendron month. The ridges of Sandakpur and Tinjure–Milke–Jaljale turn red and pink, and the first flush is in full swing in Ilam and Kanyam. The Kanchenjunga and Makalu treks are in season, with warm days and some afternoon cloud. Late in the month the Baisakh full moon may bring Sakela Ubhauli to Rai villages and towns such as Dhankuta.
months.tip: Start walks at dawn; spring cloud usually rises by late morning.

months.summary: Warm and increasingly humid, with pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the afternoons. Second flush tea begins in Ilam. Early May is still good for the high treks to Pang Pema and Makalu Base Camp, with long days and fewer trekkers, but haze often hides distant peaks. Sakela Ubhauli is celebrated at the Baisakh full moon. The plains below Bhedetar become very hot.
months.tip: Finish high treks by mid-May before the monsoon reaches the eastern hills, usually early June.

months.summary: The monsoon reaches eastern Nepal first, usually in early June, and this is one of the wettest parts of the country. Hills turn deep green and tea grows fast, but cloud hides the mountains, leeches come out on the trails and landslides block roads. The high treks are not recommended. If you come, keep to Ilam's tea gardens and the main roads, with flexible plans.
months.tip: Allow extra days for road delays and expect flights to Tumlingtar to be cancelled.

months.summary: Peak monsoon. Rain falls most days, often heavily, and mist sits on the ridges. Tea gardens are at their greenest and monsoon flush leaf is picked, but views are rare and travel is slow. Landslides are common on the Mechi and Koshi highways. We do not plan treks this month, and suggest short tea-country stays only for travellers who enjoy rain.
months.tip: Carry leech socks and a good rain jacket even for short walks.

months.weather: Ilam about 19–25 °C, monsoon, breaks of sun
months.summary: Still monsoon, with some longer breaks of sunshine. Rivers are high and roads remain risky. Tea plucking continues. Some trekkers start the Kanchenjunga or Makalu treks late in the month to reach the high country in September, but trails are wet and leechy below 2,500 m. For most travellers it is a month to skip in the east.
months.tip: If you must travel, fly rather than drive where possible.

months.weather: Ilam about 17–24 °C, monsoon easing, clearing late
months.summary: The monsoon eases through the month and the hills dry out. Late September brings the first clear mornings and the start of trekking season. Dashain's Navaratri may begin in late September, bringing pilgrims to Pathibhara and families travelling home across the region. Expect busy buses and full flights around the festival.
months.tip: Check Dashain dates before booking; transport and offices are disrupted for several days.

months.summary: The best month for the high treks. Skies clear, the air is crisp, and the Kanchenjunga and Makalu trails are in prime condition. Pathibhara is busy around Dashain, and autumn flush tea begins in Ilam. Sandakpur gives its best four-peak views from now until December. Book flights and lodges early around Dashain and Tihar.
months.tip: Plan your trek dates around Dashain and Tihar, when guides and porters go home.

months.summary: Clear, dry and settled: excellent for everything from Ilam's tea gardens to Pang Pema. Nights in the high country are very cold. Oranges ripen around Dhankuta. Late November or December brings the Mangsir full moon, with Chasok Tangnam for the Limbu and Sakela Udhauli for the Rai. Sandakpur's views are at their best.
months.tip: Ask us to time your trip to the Mangsir full moon to see Chasok Tangnam or Sakela.

months.weather: Ilam about 5–17 °C, dry, clear, cold nights
months.summary: Cold and clear. The high treks close as snow and cold set in, though early December is still possible for well-equipped groups. The hills are at their quietest, with sunny days, orange harvests in Dhankuta and clear views from Sandakpur and Antu Danda. The Mangsir full moon often falls in December, bringing Chasok Tangnam, Sakela Udhauli and Yomari Punhi in Newar bazaars such as Chainpur.
months.tip: Bring a sleeping bag rated to minus 10 °C or lower for any night above 3,000 m.

faqs.a: Yes, especially if you have already seen Kathmandu and the Annapurnas or Everest, or want quiet. Eastern Nepal has Ilam's tea gardens, the Sandakpur view of four eight-thousanders, the remote Kanchenjunga and Makalu treks, and Kirat Rai and Limbu culture, with far fewer tourists than the west.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit eastern Nepal?
faqs.a: October and November are best for clear views and the high treks. March to May brings rhododendrons, tea plucking and good trekking with more haze. December to February is cold but clear in the hills. June to September is a heavy monsoon here, with landslides and leeches.

faqs.q: How do I get to eastern Nepal from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly to Bhadrapur for Ilam and Kanyam, Biratnagar for Dharan, Dhankuta and Hile, or Tumlingtar for Chainpur and Makalu. Flights take 40–50 minutes. By road, overnight buses reach the eastern towns in 10–16 hours. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for eastern Nepal?
faqs.a: A week covers Ilam, Kanyam and Sandakpur. Ten days adds Dhankuta, Hile and Bhedetar or Chainpur. The Kanchenjunga North trek to Pang Pema needs about 18–22 days, and Makalu Base Camp about 16–20 days from Kathmandu.

faqs.q: Do I need permits for eastern Nepal?
faqs.a: Not for most of the region. The Kanchenjunga trek needs a conservation area permit and a restricted area permit, and the Makalu trek a national park permit. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers must use a licensed guide in national parks and conservation areas. Check current status before you travel.

The Kirat are indigenous peoples of eastern Nepal, chiefly the Rai and Limbu, along with groups such as the Yakkha and Sunuwar. They have their own languages, priests and the Mundhum, an oral scripture. Their festivals include Sakela and Chasok Tangnam, both linked to the farming year.

faqs.q: Is the Kanchenjunga trek harder than Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: Generally yes. It is longer, more remote, with simpler lodges and fewer rescue options, and requires a restricted area permit with a licensed guide. Maximum altitudes are similar. It suits trekkers who have already done a high-altitude trek.

faqs.q: Can I see Everest from eastern Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes, from Sandakpur on the Singalila ridge in Ilam district, where on clear mornings Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga are all visible. Everest is far away, more than 100 km, so it looks smaller than Kanchenjunga, which fills the northern horizon.

faqs.q: Is eastern Nepal safe for travellers?
faqs.a: Eastern Nepal is generally safe and friendly for travellers, including solo women. The main risks are road travel on steep hill roads, monsoon landslides, and altitude on the high treks. Travel with a licensed guide in remote areas and carry insurance that covers helicopter evacuation.
